It runs from about one paragraph to one page and is less detailed than a project plan [5][7].
It answers the who, what, when, where and why, while the plan covers how the work gets done [6].

points: Give the reader a numbered list they can follow in about 30 minutes, built from the TeamGantt and Asana steps [6][7].

h3.title: 1. Summarize the project and its purpose
points: Say what the project is, why it is happening now and what problem it solves [6][8].
Keep it to one or two short paragraphs.

h3.title: 2. Set goals and success measures

Write measurable goals; the Google AI overview suggests SMART goals tied to larger business goals [8].

h3.title: 3. Add background and audience
points: Give context your stakeholders might not have, such as why you are working on this and what business need it meets [7].
Name the target audience and add client background if the team is new to the client [6][7].

h3.title: 4. Name the people and their roles

h3.title: 5. List deliverables with dates
points: Include a projected start and end date, plus the timing of major phases and deliverables [5].
Link to the timeline view your team already uses.

The project manager owns the brief and finishes it after working with the team and stakeholders [5][6].
Sales or an account manager may fill in a first version as part of the handoff, and the project manager makes sure it is complete [6].
Do not paste in everything sales shares, because too much detail overwhelms the team [6].
For a team lead, this usually means you write it, and the people doing the work check it before kickoff.

blocks.text: If you've got several projects running and a kickoff coming up, you probably also have notes from sales, from clients and from your own head. Without a short document that pulls them together, your team can start with different ideas of what the work is.

In this guide, we show you how to write a project brief that fits on one page and that people will actually read. You'll get the sections to include and a six-step process, and we also cover how to keep every brief consistent.
Whether you write one a month or one a week, here's how to make the next one faster.

A [project brief](https://www.smartsheet.com/content/project-brief) is a short summary of the basic elements of a project, and it lets your team share goals, strategy and timeline with stakeholders in one place.

Most briefs run from about one paragraph to one page, and they hold less detail than a [project plan](https://asana.com/resources/project-brief). Think of the brief as the quick version that people can scan before they start work.

A brief also answers the who, what, when, where and why of the work, while the plan covers [how the work gets done](https://www.teamgantt.com/resources/articles/project-brief). If you want a wider view of how briefs fit into planning, our [project management basics](https://planwise.example/blog/project-management-basics) guide is a good place to start.
Who is the brief for? Here are the readers you should have in mind as you write it:

items: Your own team needs to know what the work is and how they fit into it.
Clients need the broad strokes without every detail of how you will carry out their request.
Cross-functional collaborators need [quick alignment](https://asana.com/resources/project-brief) without reading a full plan.

blocks.text: Keeping those readers in mind helps you decide what to put in and what to leave out.

sections.h2: What to include in a project brief

blocks.text: Smartsheet says the three major elements of a [project brief](https://www.smartsheet.com/content/project-brief) are a project overview, a goal statement and an estimated timeline. [Asana](https://asana.com/resources/project-brief) lists four key elements, and [Raydyant](https://raydyant.com/blog/what-to-include-in-a-project-brief) suggests a longer set of questions.
Here is each list side by side, so you can see how the same idea gets a little more detail from one source to the next:

items: Smartsheet names the overview, the goals and the timeline.
Asana names background information, objectives and success metrics, the timeline and the target audience.
Raydyant suggests the problem, audience, current situation, desired outcome, constraints, timeline, existing systems and how success might be measured.

blocks.text: You don't need every answer on day one. As Raydyant puts it, the brief's job is to [make the important questions visible](https://raydyant.com/blog/what-to-include-in-a-project-brief) so the first conversation can be productive.

For larger projects, or readers who don't know your team, Smartsheet suggests adding more. That can include [background information, success metrics and the project's target market](https://www.smartsheet.com/content/project-brief).

Here's how to put this to use: start with the overview, goals and timeline, then add background and audience when the people reading the brief need more context. If your team runs several projects at once, keep the same core parts every time so readers know where to look.

sections.h2: How to write a project brief in six steps

blocks.text: Here's how to turn the parts above into a finished brief.
Write for the people who will read the brief, and cut anything they don't need to start work.
1. Summarize the project and its purpose
Say what the project is, why it is happening now and what problem it solves, as [TeamGantt](https://www.teamgantt.com/resources/articles/project-brief) suggests.
2. Set goals and success measures

State the objective, goals and deliverables concretely, which is how [Smartsheet](https://www.smartsheet.com/content/project-brief) says a brief should read. Write goals you can measure, and tie them to larger business goals. The Google AI overview shown with the [Smartsheet templates](https://www.smartsheet.com/content/project-brief-templates) results recommends SMART goals for this.
3. Add background and audience
Give context your stakeholders might not have, such as why you are working on this project and what business need it meets, as [Asana](https://asana.com/resources/project-brief) advises.
Then name the target audience. If the team is new to the client, add a few lines of [client background](https://www.teamgantt.com/resources/articles/project-brief) too.
4. Name the people and their roles

Introduce the key players and what each person does on the project. Say who owns the brief, since [TeamGantt](https://www.teamgantt.com/resources/articles/project-brief) says the project manager is ultimately responsible for it.
5. List deliverables with dates

Include a projected start and end date, plus the timing of major phases and deliverables, as [Smartsheet](https://www.smartsheet.com/content/project-brief) recommends. Link to the [Gantt timeline](https://planwise.example/features/gantt) your team already uses, so the dates in the brief match the dates on the schedule.
6. Note constraints, scope limits and where to find more

items: Record the constraints and existing systems that shape the work, as [Raydyant](https://raydyant.com/blog/what-to-include-in-a-project-brief) suggests.

blocks.text: If you'd like a ready-made layout for all six steps, our [project brief template](https://planwise.example/templates/project-brief) follows the same order.

[TeamGantt](https://www.teamgantt.com/resources/articles/project-brief) says the project manager should own responsibility for the brief. [Smartsheet](https://www.smartsheet.com/content/project-brief) adds that the project manager writes it after working with the team and stakeholders to settle the goals, timing and strategy of the project.
Even then, it's up to the project manager to make sure the brief is complete and that the team and stakeholders understand every part of it.

Honestly, the biggest risk in a handoff is too much detail. [TeamGantt](https://www.teamgantt.com/resources/articles/project-brief) warns that a full set of sales notes can easily overwhelm your team and stakeholders, so you need to pull out only the parts they need to start work.
For a team lead running several projects, this usually means you write the brief yourself. Here's how we suggest sharing the work:

items: Collect what sales or the account manager already knows about the project and the client.
Pick out only the goals, dates, roles and deliverables the team needs to begin.
Write the brief in one sitting so it reads as a single clear summary.
Ask the people doing the work to read it and flag anything that looks wrong or missing before kickoff.

blocks.text: This way the people who will use the brief get a say in it, and you still keep one owner for the final version.

sections.h2: Project brief vs. project plan, charter and creative brief

blocks.text: Four documents get mixed up more than any others: the project brief, the project plan, the project charter and the creative brief. Knowing what each one does helps you pick the right one for the job in front of you.

A [project plan](https://asana.com/resources/project-brief) holds the full detail, while your brief is a condensed version of it. [TeamGantt](https://www.teamgantt.com/resources/articles/project-brief) puts it this way: the plan details how a project will get done, and the brief defines the who, what, when, where and why.

A [project charter](https://www.teamgantt.com/resources/articles/project-brief) is longer and more formal, and it goes into all the extra information you left out of the brief. [Asana](https://asana.com/resources/project-brief) adds that a charter formally authorizes a project and gives the project manager authority to allocate resources.
If your project includes creative work, you will likely write both, and the project brief paints the broad strokes of the whole project.

An executive summary is a fourth option. According to [Asana](https://asana.com/resources/project-brief), it suits expansive projects with C-suite stakeholders or cases where you have drafted a business case.
The table below sets the five documents side by side, and the right choice depends on who will read it and what you need from them.

rows: Details how the project will get done
Formally authorizes the project and the manager's authority to use resources
Gives detailed direction for creative work
Design, copy and other creative tasks

sections.h2: Tips to keep your brief useful

blocks.text: Once your brief is written, a few habits keep it useful for the whole project, and here's how to make it something your team actually opens.

items: Keep it to one page, because [TeamGantt](https://www.teamgantt.com/resources/articles/project-brief) suggests challenging yourself to stay within that limit so people will want to reference it.
Refresh the brief whenever project details change, because [Smartsheet](https://www.smartsheet.com/content/project-brief) says a brief should be as up to date as possible.
Turn it into a kickoff slide by condensing the brief into a few bullets, which [Smartsheet](https://www.smartsheet.com/content/project-brief) says works well for presentations and kickoff meetings.

Rewrite it in the past tense after the project ends to make a short case study you can share with potential clients or investors, as [Smartsheet](https://www.smartsheet.com/content/project-brief) describes.

blocks.text: When should you write the brief?

The sources give different answers here. [Smartsheet](https://www.smartsheet.com/content/project-brief) says to write the brief after you've finalized the project details, while [TeamGantt](https://www.teamgantt.com/resources/articles/project-brief) and [Asana](https://asana.com/resources/project-brief) say to write it at the very start of the project.
Honestly, both ideas can work together, so we suggest this approach, which combines the sources and is our own recommendation:

items: Write a first draft at the start, before your internal kickoff meeting, so everyone begins with the same picture.
Mark any open questions in the draft so your team knows what is still being decided.
Update the brief once the details settle, then share the final version with your stakeholders so it matches the finished plan.

blocks.text: With this approach, your team gets context on day one, and your stakeholders still receive a brief that matches the finished plan.

sections.h2: How to keep briefs consistent across several projects

blocks.text: If you run several projects at once, writing a fresh brief in a new shape every time costs you hours and can confuse the people who read them. Luckily, a repeatable format can take away much of that extra work.
Here's how you can set that up for your own team.

items: Pick one format and use it for every project, so your team never has to learn a new layout.
Keep the same sections in the same order, so readers know exactly where to find the goal and the dates.
Link each brief to the timeline and the [Kanban board](https://planwise.example/features/kanban) your team already uses, so the dates and tasks match what the brief says.
Review each brief whenever the scope or the dates change, because Smartsheet says a brief should be [as up to date as possible](https://www.smartsheet.com/content/project-brief).

blocks.text: We think this works because a brief that looks the same every time is easier for stakeholders to scan and for your team to find things in as they move between projects.
To get started, you can take the sections you already use in your best brief and save that as your standard. Then ask your team which section they check first, and put it at the top.

You now have what you need to write a brief that your team will read and use, and the best way to make it stick is to write one for a project you are running today. Honestly, seeing how the format feels on real work teaches more than any guide can.

Open the [Planwise project brief template](https://planwise.example/templates/project-brief) and work through the six steps for one current project. As [TeamGantt](https://www.teamgantt.com/resources/articles/project-brief) suggests, challenge yourself to keep it to one page, so people will want to reference it.
Here's how to finish it before your next kickoff:

items: Fill in the summary, goals, background, roles, deliverables and constraints for one live project.
Add your deliverable dates to a Gantt view, so you can see how the milestones line up with the rest of your work.
Share the brief with your team and your stakeholders, and ask each person to confirm the part that affects them.

blocks.text: A brief that is already written, shared and checked before kickoff gives everyone the same starting point, and you can reuse the same format for your next project by changing only the details. Why not start with the project on your desk right now?
What is a project brief for?

A project brief shares the key goals, scope and timeline with your team and stakeholders so everyone starts with the same understanding. [Smartsheet](https://www.smartsheet.com/content/project-brief) describes it as a way to share goals, strategy and timelines, and [TeamGantt](https://www.teamgantt.com/resources/articles/project-brief) says it creates alignment so people know what to expect and how they'll be involved.
How long should a project brief be?

Most guides say a brief runs from about one paragraph to one page, and [TeamGantt](https://www.teamgantt.com/resources/articles/project-brief) suggests aiming for one page so people will want to use it. [Asana](https://asana.com/resources/project-brief) agrees that some briefs are as short as a paragraph and others run up to a page.
How do you write a project brief?

Work through six steps: summarize the project and its purpose, set goals and success measures, add background and audience, name the people and their roles, list deliverables with dates, and note scope limits or constraints.
Who writes a project brief?

The project manager owns the brief and writes it after working with the team and stakeholders on goals, timing and strategy, as [Smartsheet](https://www.smartsheet.com/content/project-brief) explains. Your sales team or an account manager may start a first version as part of the handoff, and [TeamGantt](https://www.teamgantt.com/resources/articles/project-brief) notes that the project manager makes sure it is complete.
What is the difference between a project brief and a project charter?

A brief is a high-level summary, while a charter is longer, more formal and goes into the extra detail the brief leaves out, according to [TeamGantt](https://www.teamgantt.com/resources/articles/project-brief). [Asana](https://asana.com/resources/project-brief) adds that a charter formally authorizes a project and gives the project manager authority to allocate resources. Use a brief when you want a quick reference that aligns your team.
